Many separate database queries are made, which can be slow for large models.

terms.meaning: a connection used to read and write stored data during one request.

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Imports and optional PDF setup
sections.what: Loads the web tools, the database, the Excel writer, and tries to load the PDF writer, recording whether that worked.
sections.why: Likely reason: the PDF library may not be installed, and a failed import should not stop the whole app.
sections.watch_out: If the PDF import fails for any reason, PDF is silently turned off, as the HAS_PDF flag shows.

sections.name: export_excel (part 1)
sections.title: Loading a scenario's data
sections.what: Loads the scenario, its model, time periods, drivers, driver values, segments, lines, line inputs and stored results. Stops with a not-found error if the scenario or model is missing.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: If no results were calculated, the result lists are simply empty, and the export will still succeed.

sections.name: export_excel (part 2)
sections.title: Shaping data for the Excel writer
sections.what: Sorts the loaded data into the plain shapes the Excel writer expects: model details, driver values by year, and each line's base volume and price.
sections.why: Likely reason: the Excel writer uses plain dictionaries so it does not depend on the database.
sections.watch_out: Base volume and price are read only from inputs named Base_Vol_Y0 and Base_Price_Y0. Other names are ignored.

sections.name: export_excel (part 3)
sections.title: Adding lines and results
sections.what: Adds each active line's details, then builds yearly financial statement figures and valuation figures. Missing numbers are treated as zero.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: A missing value becomes zero rather than blank, so a real gap can look like a real figure.

sections.name: export_excel (part 4)
sections.title: Writing and returning the Excel file
sections.what: Builds a clean file name from the model and scenario names, writes the Excel file to the temp folder, and returns it as a download.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: The same scenario always gets the same file name, so a new export overwrites the older file.

sections.name: export_pdf
sections.title: PDF export placeholder
sections.what: Reports whether the PDF library is installed and returns a message in every case. No PDF is produced.
sections.why: Likely reason: a placeholder for a future PDF feature.
sections.watch_out: A caller may expect a file and receive only a message.

summary: Creates Excel files from a saved scenario by gathering its data from the database, and holds a placeholder for PDF export.
purpose: Let the user download a scenario as a spreadsheet they can open and review.
why: Likely reason: the spreadsheet is the main output for financial models. PDF is optional because its library may not be installed.
how: Finds the scenario, its model, time periods, drivers, segments, lines, inputs and stored results. Packs them into plain dictionaries, writes an Excel file to the temp folder with a cleaned-up name, and returns it. The PDF route only reports whether the optional PDF library is present.
inputs: A scenario id in the web address, read from the database.
outputs: An Excel file download. For PDF, a JSON message.
risks: Files are written to the temp folder and never deleted here. Missing results are shown as zero, which can hide that no calculation was run. The PDF route does not produce a PDF.
debug: If the file shows only zeros, check whether results exist in the database for that scenario. A 404 means the scenario or model id is wrong. If the Excel writer fails, the error text is returned; check the export module.
